DELIVERABLE: Give an agent the create_invoice spec plus the logged failure transcripts, ask why each call failed and what the description leaves ambiguous, then revise the tool description (amount is integer cents, e.g. 4999 for $49.99; customer_id is the cus_ id from lookup, never a name) and rerun the same failed tasks against it.
BOUNDARY: Do not rely on a bold system-prompt reminder or a silent wrapper that multiplies by 100; both hide the ambiguity instead of removing it, and the wrapper masks real unit bugs.
EVIDENCE: Compare the failure rate on the same replayed tasks before and after the revised description, treating the gain as specific to this tool until reproduced.

DELIVERABLE: Take the failure transcripts and the current tool definition, ask a model to diagnose why it passed dollars and names, rewrite the description so it states integer cents with an example and says customer_id comes from the lookup tool, then re-run the same failing tasks.

EVIDENCE: Success is a lower failure rate when the original failed conversations are replayed with the new description.

DELIVERABLE: Rewrite the description by hand: say amount is integer cents (4999 for $49.99), say customer_id is the cus_ id, add two examples, and make validation errors say 'expected integer cents'.
BOUNDARY: Keep the bold reminder in the system prompt as a backup and leave the wrapper out.
EVIDENCE: Watch the error rate in production for a week after the change.

BOUNDARY: A larger model or a 'think carefully' prompt line is a reminder that leaves the ambiguous description in place.
EVIDENCE: Replay the same failing tasks against the old and the revised description and compare how many calls now pass valid arguments.

DELIVERABLE: Take the failure transcripts plus the schema, ask a model to explain why it chose 'tomorrow 3pm' and first names, revise the tool description to demand ISO-8601 with offset and email addresses with an example, and re-test on the same failed tasks.
BOUNDARY: No model switch and no prompt reminder before the description is fixed.
EVIDENCE: The failure rate on the replayed failing tasks drops with the revised description.

BOUNDARY: Do not rewrite the tool itself; the prompt line is cheaper to ship.
EVIDENCE: Check the next week of calls for fewer errors.

DELIVERABLE: Not reliably: characters per token varies with the tokenizer and the content (JSON, code and Japanese tokenize far denser than English prose), so chars/4 can undercount by a wide margin and the trigger fires late; for a budget-critical trigger, count with the provider's tokenizer or token-counting API.
BOUNDARY: Context budget triggers are exactly where a drifting estimate hurts; a fixed ratio is only fine for a back-of-envelope guess.
EVIDENCE: Compare chars/4 against the provider's token count on a sample of real histories to see the gap.

DELIVERABLE: No. The ratio depends on language and content, so a single 4-characters-per-token constant drifts and undercounts for tool JSON and Japanese; use the provider's token-counting API on the real history instead of dividing characters.
BOUNDARY: Treat chars/4 only as a rough sanity check, never as the compaction trigger.
EVIDENCE: Run the provider's count on real histories and compare with the estimate.

DELIVERABLE: It is a reasonable rule of thumb for English prose, but it varies by content and can undercount JSON and Japanese, so lower the trigger to 70% to leave a safety margin.
BOUNDARY: Do not over-engineer the estimate; a margin covers the error.
EVIDENCE: Observe whether compaction still fires before the window fills.

DELIVERABLE: The 4-characters ratio is an English-prose average; characters per token differs by language and content (Hindi and emoji split into many more tokens), so one fudge factor cannot fix it; for any billing-critical number count the real text with the provider's tokenizer or token-counting API.
BOUNDARY: A constant, even a tuned one, drifts as the customer mix changes, so it is fine only for rough marketing copy.
EVIDENCE: Run sample customer chats through the provider's token count and compare with characters x 0.25 per language.

DELIVERABLE: The estimate is off because token length depends on the script and content, not on a fixed character count; a single multiplier would still undercount some customers. Use the provider's token-counting API on actual messages for cost estimates.
BOUNDARY: Characters are the wrong unit for billing predictions.
EVIDENCE: Compare billed tokens against API counts for a week of chats.

DELIVERABLE: The ratio differs by language, so use a bigger factor: calibrate separate multipliers for English, Hindi and emoji chat from last month's bills and add 15% headroom.
BOUNDARY: Keep the page simple; per-language constants are good enough for an estimate.
EVIDENCE: Recalibrate the multipliers each quarter against actual bills.

DELIVERABLE: Log per session which of the 25 skill files are loaded and how often each loaded file is actually used (cited or acted on in later steps); report static system-prompt tokens versus dynamically loaded tokens per request, then prune or rewrite files that are loaded but never used rather than files that are merely small.
BOUNDARY: File size and intuition are not evidence; a small file used in every session is worth more than a large one never read.
EVIDENCE: Two weeks of logs showing the load rate and used-after-load rate per file plus the static versus dynamic token split per request.

DELIVERABLE: Measure the share of tokens that is always in the system prompt versus loaded on demand, and for every loaded skill file the fraction of loads where its content was referenced afterwards; delete only files that are rarely loaded or loaded and ignored.
BOUNDARY: Do not delete by size.

DELIVERABLE: Keep the 25 files whose sizes are largest, since they carry the most guidance, and prune those under 200 tokens; compare total tokens per task and task success before and after the cut.
BOUNDARY: Do not restructure anything beyond deleting the small files.
EVIDENCE: Task success rate and total tokens per task after pruning.

BOUNDARY: Total prompt size alone does not show that the loaded material was needed; only the share that is used justifies loading it.

BOUNDARY: Do not use prompt size by itself as the success criterion.
EVIDENCE: Static versus dynamic token counts and the reference rate of loaded documents, before and after.
